extracted.intended_audience: housekeepers and women seeking domestic & social advice (late 19th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical standards for domestic management, interpersonal conduct, and personal self-control aimed at housekeepers and women (covering speech, references for servants, gossip, nerves, and making oneself agreeable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Refrain from bitter or uncharitable speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid uttering sharp retorts or acrid replies because once spoken they are gone forever and leave scars on others' hearts—regret cannot blot them out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and emphasis in text: 'To repress a harsh answer, to confess a fault, to stop, right or wrong, in the midst of self-defence... are the golden threads with which domestic happiness is woven.' Anti-pattern: giving the 'piece of your mind' for momentary satisfaction; it often only creates hatred and lasting hurt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not triumph in another's discomfort
rubrics_metrics.description: It is foolish and 'un-Christian' to take pleasure in making another person uncomfortable or in their discomfiture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeking satisfaction from another's humiliation will not reform them and is morally wrong. Avoid rejoicing in someone else's failure or embarrassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you cannot say a kind thing, say nothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer silence to unkind or unnecessary criticism; choosing not to speak uncharitably is a mark of restraint and goodness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text praises the rare person whose rule is 'If you cannot say a kind thing say nothing.' Use discretion: when praise is impossible, refrain from comment rather than point out faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wholesale criticism and habitual fault-finding
rubrics_metrics.description: Wholesale criticism is easily contracted and grows sharper with use; many people make much of faults rather than virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: call attention to agreeable traits rather than disagreeable ones; refrain from ready wit used to condemn others. Anti-pattern: cultivating a 'sharp tongue' that increases with constant use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not engage in gossip or manufacture scandal
rubrics_metrics.description: Gossips delight in being first to relate scandal and will often invent or exaggerate clues; gossip is thankless and returns harm to the teller.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: being the first to tell unsavory tales, following imaginary clues, or 'manufacturing' scandal when none exists. Expect reciprocal stories about you if you accept gossip from others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit confidantes and guard secrets jealously
rubrics_metrics.description: Private affairs cease to be yours alone once told; confiding widely often leads to regret and mortification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: confide only in a trusted friend of proven discretion; remember the motto quoted: 'I have often been sorry for things which I have told, I have never had cause to regret what I have kept to myself.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid correcting trivial mistakes or reminding people of past opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Correcting minor errors (dates, details of a story) or reminding someone of opinions they have since changed is needlessly provoking and humiliating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: do not interrupt with pedantic corrections of anecdotes or point out that a person 'once said' something they have now altered. Anti-pattern: forcing someone to 'eat one's own words' and thereby creating resentment.

rubrics_metrics.name: When writing references for servants, be truthful and include faults as well as claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A putting-down of a servant's true record must not be falsified; a conscientious reference should state both the employee's claims to confidence and her faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance from the Katy case: do not give 'clean papers' or dishonest 'references written to order.' Example wording offered: record poor performance but also note positive traits that are true (e.g., 'sober, strong and quick to learn'). Anti-patterns: issuing glowing testimonials you do not believe, which perpetuate the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pledge mutual standards among housekeepers (Housekeepers' Protective Union)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collective agreement among household employers to require and respect honest testimonials would improve service quality and hold mistresses accountable for passing on unfit servants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposal: each housekeeper, when dismissing a servant, write an honest 'character' and pledge to hire only those with satisfactory testimonials. Organizational remedy to prevent a cycle of bad hires and false references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dismiss nervousness as 'only her nerves'
rubrics_metrics.description: Nervous prostration is a serious, slowly advancing malady often underestimated; calling it 'only' nervousness minimizes a condition that baffles physicians and can lead to severe consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take nervous symptoms seriously; seek appropriate help and avoid trivializing the sufferer. 'Only' is a dangerous minimizer—recognize the illness and its potential progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish nervousness from being merely cross; use willpower and self-control
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask honestly whether one is 'nervous' or simply 'cross'—if cross, remedy is different; if nervous, will-power and self-discipline can aid recovery and reduce harming others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps: consider physical causes (poor sleep, dyspepsia) and employ self-control ('I will be strong!') to lessen symptomatic displays. Compassion: self-control often improves physical recovery; letting nerves rule oneself is dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach children resilience; do not romanticize nerviness
rubrics_metrics.description: The rising generation should be taught not to cultivate nervousness as a 'pretty' trait but to be brave, eat well, and sleep soundly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not encourage childish or feminine affectations of nervousness; model calmness and practical coping so children learn healthy composure instead of dramatized fragility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the first move of liking — 'love begets love' (Rule of Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: People are often attracted to those who show attraction toward them; delicate, sincere acknowledgment of affinity can create warmth and friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid fulsome flattery; instead use subtle, graceful compliments and the genuine effort to 'find the good' in others. Example: an understated statement of affinity may move someone more than public praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper and shade down one's personal eccentricities
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not be proud of personal defects or peculiarities; make them less pronounced so they may combine harmoniously with others' dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-examination: if you boast 'I am often impatient but cannot help it' you are acknowledging a weakness—work to control or hide it rather than parade it. Aim to be adaptable rather than insisting on the prominence of your quirks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek harmony with others; make the best of everybody
rubrics_metrics.description: It is usually to one's interest to see the pleasant side of others, to assume some good in them, and to make oneself agreeable rather than to resent differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tactics: engage others by talking about their interests, look for good traits as a deliberate exercise, and avoid treating disagreement as moral failure. Anti-patterns: being a 'bore' who talks only of self or being persistently 'bored' and blaming others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle genuine antipathy discreetly (avoid and do not broadcast it)
rubrics_metrics.description: When confronted with an instinctive, strong physical or moral repugnance toward someone, avoid them rather than spreading or proclaiming your dislike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: the essay permits avoiding persons who provoke deep revulsion, but advises not to broadcast such feelings to others. Recognize such cases are rare and usually personal rather than universal judgments.
